title: Build a cube from six magnetic building tiles: stand four walls on the base so their edges catch, then lower the lid on
instruction: Build a closed cube from the six square tiles: stand four of the tiles from the rack on the edges of the flat tile so their magnets catch, then put the last one on top as the lid.
context: Magnetic building tiles are among the commonest toys in homes and nurseries with young children, and a cube is the first thing a child builds and the first thing an adult builds for them. The tiles join only by small magnets inside their edges. A wall has to be stood on the base's edge square to it and brought within about 3 mm for the magnets to catch; let go further off, skewed or tilted, it falls over or flat. Each wall stands only by that light hold (it tips over past a few degrees of lean), so the walls already up are knocked down by a careless touch while the next one goes in beside them, and the fourth wall must slip in between two standing walls. The lid has to come down square on all four top edges at once; dropped from a height or skewed it lands on one edge, catches crooked or pushes a wall out.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. 1) Six square tiles from one MAGNA-TILES Classic 32-Piece Set (item 02132; any six of its 14 squares): 76.2 across (the maker's 3-inch squares), 6 thick (estimate), 32 g each (a published weighing), two ceramic magnets in each edge, edges rounded so two tiles meet edge to edge at any angle. 2) The base: one tile lies flat on the bare table with its centre at (140, -65) and its edges along x and y. 3) The other five stand on edge, faces toward the robot, in alternate slots of a two-piece bamboo plate rack (two slotted bars laid side by side, 30 apart, along x, centred on y = -210; slots 0.8 in (20.3) apart; the simulation's slots are 8 wide and 24 deep, estimates: measure the real rack, a wider slot lets each tile lean further), in the slots centred at x = 100, 141, 181, 222 and 262, standing upright or leaning a few degrees in its slot (a 6 mm tile lying flat cannot be pinched off a table, so the loose tiles stand on edge with their top edge free). No mat. Frictions (estimates): tile on tile 0.45, tile on table 0.35, bamboo 0.5. Start: both arms at their ready pose, grippers open.
scoring: Judged after the run from the trial video and a photo, then a lift test. An edge is joined when the two tiles meet along it with no gap (in simulation: both magnets of that edge within 3 mm of the other tile's). A wall stands: within 10 degrees of upright, joined to the base. Tiles count only when both grippers are at least 3 cm from them and no tile has moved over the last second. Lift test (real trial, after the robot has let go): pinch the cube's top at two opposite edges and lift it 5 cm for 2 s; it stays together only if every edge is joined. It is done once, after the photo: if only the lid comes away, the score is 0.75; if a wall or the base comes away, that wall's edges count as not joined (at most 0.25). 1.0: closed cube: base, four walls and lid, all 12 edges joined (it passes the lift test). 0.75: base, four walls and all 8 of their edges joined, with the lid lying on top within 15 mm of centre but not joined on all four edges (it fails the lift test). 0.5: base and four walls with all 8 edges joined, no lid on top. 0.25: one to four walls standing joined to the base, but not all 8 wall edges joined. A lid that misses, falls off or falls inside leaves the score of the walls still standing (0.5 if all four stand joined). 0: no wall standing joined to the base, or the base no longer lying flat on the table. Doing nothing scores 0.
reset_notes: About 1 minute. Pull the cube apart (wall by wall; the magnets let go with a light pull) and pick up any fallen tile. Lay one tile flat at the base's place, edges along x and y, and stand the other five on edge in the five alternate rack slots, faces toward the robot. Use the same six squares every trial. Return both arms to the ready pose.
fidelity: Tiles are rigid slabs at true size and mass; the rounded rim is two 45-degree chamfers. Each edge's two magnets are two attracting points, applied as forces every physics step, no joints: a corner edge takes 1.4 N to pull off and pulls a tile's weight from a 3 mm gap (estimates from published hang tests). The rack's slot sizes and all frictions are estimates.
